1.answer: The receiver records when each signal arrives. Each signal carries its send time, so the travel time is the receive time minus the send time. Multiplying the travel time by the speed of light c gives the distance to that satellite.
1.quote: Your receiver notes when the signal arrives. The **travel time** is receive time minus send time.

2.answer: A cheap receiver clock is wrong by some unknown amount, and that error adds the same amount (c·b) to every distance. The clock bias b becomes a fourth unknown alongside x, y and z. Four unknowns need four equations, so the receiver needs four satellites.
2.quote: There are four unknowns (x, y, z, b), so the receiver needs four equations: four satellites.

3.answer: Two effects change the satellite clock rate. Speed slows it by about 7 µs per day, and weaker gravity speeds it up by about 45 µs per day. The net result is that satellite clocks gain about 38 µs per day. Multiplied by c, that is about 11 km of distance per day. The system needs its clocks to agree within a few nanoseconds, and the drift reaches 26 ns (8 m) after just one minute.
3.quote: 38 µs looks small. Multiply by c: 38 µs × 300 m per µs ≈ 11 km.

4.answer: Each distance would be off by about 300 m (1 µs × c). Since the clock is fast, the distances would come out too long. With only three satellites, nothing absorbs this error, so the spheres would not meet at the true position.
4.quote: Then every distance is wrong by 1 ms × c = 300 km. The three spheres no longer meet at your true position.
